summary:
Ceará stands under Brazil's national framework; the national record carries the federal law, passport and marker rules, health-system rules and custodial resolutions. What follows is the state-level layer.

Ceará recorded 11 killings of trans people in 2024, the highest count of any state in the Northeast and the third highest nationally, according to the ANTRA dossier reported on 28 January 2025. The state has about 9.2 million residents, which the source puts at roughly 0.12 killings per 100,000 residents. Ceará's general homicide rate is not in the source inventory, so the two cannot be compared here, and the national ranking is by raw count, which tracks population size rather than risk. The ninth ANTRA dossier, reported on 26 January 2026, recorded 8 killings in Ceará in 2025, level with Minas Gerais at the top of the state ranking, or about 0.09 per 100,000 residents on the source's own figures. Both counts come from a dossier that compiles media-reported killings.

Law No. 17,480, sanctioned by Governor Camilo Santana and published on 19 May 2021, requires public and private establishments in Ceará, from 90 days after publication, to display a notice of at least 50 cm by 50 cm on the exterior or at an entrance stating that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is expressly prohibited, and listing the phone number of the Special Coordination for LGBT Public Policies for complaints, clarifications and reports. No enforcement actions, penalties or compliance data under the law are sourced.

On 7 March 2013 the state general attorney, Francisco Sales Neto, issued decision 02/2013 obligating all notaries in Ceará to accept same-sex marriages, effective 15 March 2013. For a trans visitor whose relationship or identity documents are read under birth-sex status, that notarial obligation is the operative state-level guarantee; no Ceará-specific rule on how a notary handles a trans partner's documents is sourced.

On 22 May 2024 the Court of Justice of Ceará authorized Brune Bonassi to rectify documents to reflect a neutral gender, the first non-binary person in the state to obtain such a rectification. On 29 May 2024 the state was reported to be issuing its first birth certificate recognising a person as non-binary. Whether the two concern the same person is not stated.

On 16 November 2006 Governor Lúcio Alcântara signed a law requiring educational material on sexual orientation to be included in the training of Ceará's Civil and Military Police, published in the Official Gazette on 26 November 2006. How the requirement is applied today is not recorded.

On 12 December 2017 the Sobral municipal chamber approved Bill No. 2154/17, introduced by Councillor Adauto Izidoro Arruda, prohibiting pedagogical activities that reproduce the concept of "gender ideology" or any discussion of gender diversity in all municipal and private schools in Sobral. It passed by majority with the sole opposing vote from Councillor Maria Socorro Brasileiro Magalhães and was sent to Mayor Ivo Gomes. Whether it was signed or vetoed is not recorded.
tangentialFactors:
The state's protective measures and its killing counts sit in the same record without an explanation of the gap. Ceará has a signage duty on premises, a notarial access decision from 2013, a police-training requirement from 2006 and a court route to document rectification, while the ANTRA dossier places it at the top of the 2025 state ranking by raw count. No Ceará prosecution, conviction or compliance data appears that would show how the protective measures operate in practice.

Raw-count rankings are the only comparison the inventory supports. Ceará's 8 killings in 2025 are level with Minas Gerais, but no population denominator for Minas Gerais is given, so the two cannot be compared per capita; Ceará's own per-capita figure is supplied by the source, and the state's general homicide rate is absent, so the trans-specific rate cannot be set against the background rate.

The Sobral bill runs against the state-level direction: a municipal chamber moved to bar discussion of gender diversity in schools in the same state that requires anti-discrimination notices in establishments. The outcome of that bill is not recorded.
localsOnly:
Residents of Ceará have a state reporting channel for discrimination: the Special Coordination for LGBT Public Policies, whose phone number Law No. 17,480 requires establishments to display. The duty falls on public and private premises, so it applies to businesses residents use day to day, not only to venues visitors frequent.

Document rectification runs through the Court of Justice of Ceará. The 22 May 2024 authorization for a neutral gender entry was the first of its kind in the state, and the state was issuing its first non-binary birth certificate within the same week.

Notaries in Ceará have been bound to accept same-sex marriages since 15 March 2013 under decision 02/2013 of the state general attorney. No state-level guidance is sourced on how a notary should treat a trans person's documents where the record and the person's presentation differ.

Police training in the state has been required to include material on sexual orientation since a law signed on 16 November 2006. Whether the requirement is currently enforced, and what the training covers on gender identity, is not recorded.

School policy is contested at municipal level. Sobral's chamber approved a bill in December 2017 barring discussion of gender diversity in municipal and private schools; whether the mayor signed or vetoed it is not recorded.
outOfScopeNotes:
The fate of Sobral Bill No. 2154/17 is unresolved: it was forwarded to the mayor on 12 December 2017 and no sanction or veto is recorded.

Whether the 22 May 2024 neutral-gender rectification and the 29 May 2024 non-binary birth certificate concern the same person is not stated.

No Ceará-specific custodial or prison-housing practice for trans people appears in the inventory. The material available on that subject is national in scope, is internally inconsistent between sources, and is carried by the national record.

No enforcement, penalty or compliance data for Law No. 17,480 is sourced, and no general homicide rate for Ceará is in the inventory, so the trans killing counts cannot be compared with the background rate for the state.

The ANTRA counts rest on media-reported killings; no Ceará-specific methodology note or undercount assessment is given.
